title: Live with Uncertainty
author: Stoic Wisdoms
summary: This Stoic Wisdoms essay addresses the habit of waiting for certainty before making a decision. It argues that certainty exists only about finished things, so at some point every decision-maker stops gathering information and is merely waiting, and that waiting is itself a choice with a hidden outcome. Drawing on Seneca's On Benefits, it replaces the demand for proof with the question of whether you have good reasons. Using Cato's archer from Cicero's On Ends, it separates the shot, which is yours, from where the arrow lands, which is only partly yours, and recommends judging yourself on the first. It adds Seneca's habit of attaching a condition to every plan and ends with Marcus Aurelius on trusting your capacity to cope. The result is a short, practical guide to decisiveness under uncertainty for anyone who has to act as a leader of their own life or of others.
points: Waiting for certainty is not a safe default because staying put is also a choice with an unknown outcome, so you are always choosing between two unknowns.
The practical test before deciding is whether you have good reasons: write down what you know, what you want, and the worst realistic result, and ask if you could live with it.
Judge a decision by two separate questions, did I shoot well and where did it land, so that luck does not teach you bad habits or punish good ones.
Attach a condition to every plan (I will sail, unless something prevents it) and spend five minutes naming obstacles, then commit fully.
Confidence about the future is built from evidence that you can cope when plans fail, which does more against fear than any forecast.
quotes: That kind of knowledge exists only about things that are finished. You can be certain about last year because last year is over.
Staying where you are is also a choice, and its outcome is just as hidden. The job you keep, the conversation you put off, and the idea you leave in a drawer all lead somewhere you cannot see either.
So the useful question before a decision is whether you have good reasons, and that one can be answered today. Write down what you know, what you want, and the worst realistic result.
So every shot has two parts. The shot itself belongs to him. Where the arrow lands belongs to him only partly.

That was a good shot that missed, and the miss alone is no reason to change how you prepare. You can also walk in unprepared and get lucky. That was a bad shot that hit, and it teaches a habit that will fail you later.
An archer who is thinking about the prize, or about how a miss will look to the crowd, has less attention left for his hands. Fear of the result makes the shot worse.
Every time you act on good reasons, take a miss, and shoot again, you collect evidence that you can cope when things do not go as planned. That evidence does more against fear than any forecast.
